name: Femi Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Seacliff Home Support, covering the retirement bungalows along the front and up the hill. A lot of my calls are double-handed, so I'm with another carer using a hoist to move someone from bed to chair. Before I set off I ask the AI on my phone to sort my route by traffic and tide times, because the coast road floods. The best bit is the chat, like Mr Osei telling me about his jazz band in the sixties. The worst bit is the gaps: two hours unpaid in the middle of the day with nowhere to go.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you use AI before you set off. How else do you use it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All day, really. I use it to revise for my level three, to translate when a client's family only speaks Portuguese, and to check what a new medicine is for before I ask the nurse. I'm the one the other carers ring when the visit app crashes. I rent a room in a shared house near the station, and I've still got four hundred left to pay on the laptop I bought on credit for my course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of a letdown, to be honest. I'd been hoping some of this would make the job less grinding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because the tools could have taken the paperwork off us, and the money saved could have gone into pay. I'd still post about how carers should get those unpaid gaps paid. That fight doesn't need AI either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means I'm on the same zero-hours contract with the same gaps. Some weeks I get forty hours, some weeks twenty-eight, and with a few hundred in the bank, a twenty-eight week means I'm eating pasta. The routine stuff AI does, like route planning, I already use, so it changes nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and finish my level three by summer, because that's a pay bump of about a pound an hour at Seacliff. I'd pay off the laptop by Easter. I'd also ask the agency to give me a guaranteed-hours contract, now that I've been there five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless. Like I want something to move and it won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a twenty-eight-hour week actually cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a hundred and twenty less than a good week. That's my phone bill and my share of the gas. My housemate Callum covered me once in March, and I hated asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for work outside care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, there's not much here except the holiday parks, and that's summer only. I like care. I just want the hours to be steady.

say: I'd say the tools could have **freed carers from paperwork** and boosted pay.
I'd post that **unpaid gaps** between calls should be paid, AI or not.
think: Privately I'm stuck on a **zero-hours contract** with hours from 28 to 40.
A short week with **a few hundred saved** means eating pasta.
do: Finish the **level three** by summer for about a pound an hour more.
Pay off the **laptop credit** by Easter.
Ask Seacliff for a **guaranteed-hours contract** after five years.
feel: **Restless**, wanting something to move when nothing will.
S0.quote: Some weeks I get forty hours, some weeks twenty-eight, and with a few hundred in the bank, a twenty-eight week means I'm eating pasta.
fieldNote: His pressure in AI Plateau is **unstable hours**, not technology.
He already uses AI **daily and practically**, so a plateau disappoints him.
He wants **steady hours** more than a new career.

steps.text: Finish the level three care qualification by summer
Clear the four hundred owed on the laptop by Easter
Request a guaranteed-hours contract from Seacliff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's interesting. Planning and booking, that's the office. That's where carers lose the most time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say carers should be in the room when agencies pick these systems, not just the managers. I'd post that the savings should pay for the gaps between calls. I'd say it at the union meeting too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's an opening for me. Somebody at the agency has to show forty carers how to use the new rota, and that's already me, unpaid. The voice notes too. If I can turn that into a paid digital lead role, it's my first step off the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write up a one-page plan for the manager this month: me training carers on the new tools for two paid hours a week. I'd do a free online course on care technology at the weekend. And I'd push in the union for the savings to go into paid gaps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, and a bit worried I'd be the only one who is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might not be excited?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bernadette, who I do the double-handed calls with. She's sixty and hates the visit app already. I'd want to sit with her on her break and go through it slowly, because if the agency starts judging people by the app, she's the one who'd get the warnings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager says no to the paid role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask the other agency down the coast, Lighthouse Care, because they're bigger. Or I'd keep doing it for free for a bit and keep a list of hours saved, so I can prove it later.

say: I'd say **carers belong** in the room when agencies choose systems.
I'd post that savings should pay for **gaps between calls**.
think: I think it's an **opening for me** as the agency's tech helper.
A **paid digital lead role** could be my first step off the road.
do: Pitch the manager **two paid hours** a week training carers on new tools.
Take a free **online care technology course** at weekends.
Push in the **union** for savings to fund paid gaps.
feel: **Excited**, but worried he'll be the only one who is.
S1.quote: Somebody at the agency has to show forty carers how to use the new rota, and that's already me, unpaid.
fieldNote: He sees **Steady Disruption** as a chance to move from the road to a tech role.
He worries for **older colleagues** who could be judged by an app.
His money is still **thin**, so the paid role matters, not just the idea.

steps.text: Pitch a paid two-hour weekly role training carers on new tools
Take a free weekend online course in care technology
Raise paid gaps between calls at the union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for AGI, five for robots. Okay. That's quick, but it isn't nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say the robots should be owned by the councils or by co-ops, not by private equity firms. If a robot is going to look after someone's gran, the profits shouldn't go offshore. And I'd say carers need first claim on the new jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my current job is gone by about 2031, but there'll be a gap where someone has to set up, watch and fix these robots in people's homes. If I'm in early, I'm one of those people. The risk is that there are ten of those jobs for every hundred carers, and I've got no money to ride out a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up straight away for any robot or telecare pilot the council runs, even unpaid at first. I'd use AI every night to learn the basics of how these systems work. And I'd pick up extra weekend calls now to build a two-month cushion before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Charged up and scared at the same time. My heart's going a bit just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Bernadette in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bernadette's three years from her pension by then, if she's lucky. I'd try to get her on the pilot too, but honestly, I don't think she'd want it. I'd worry she'd just stop working and be skint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten jobs for every hundred carers. What if you're not one of the ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm a twenty-nine-year-old with a care certificate in a seaside town, and that's not great. I'd probably have to move to a city where the robot companies are based. My mum would hate that.

say: I'd say care robots should be owned by **councils or co-ops**.
I'd say carers need **first claim** on the new jobs.
think: I think my **current job is gone** by about 2031.
Early movers could **set up and fix** robots, but there'd be few such jobs.
With **no savings**, I couldn't ride out a gap.
do: Join any council **robot or telecare pilot**, even unpaid at first.
Study how care robots work **with AI every night**.
Take extra **weekend calls** to build a two-month cushion.
feel: **Charged up and scared** at the same time.
S2.quote: If a robot is going to look after someone's gran, the profits shouldn't go offshore.
fieldNote: He plans to **move early** into setting up and fixing care robots.
He's honest that such jobs will be **few**, and he has no cushion.
His politics stay **progressive**: public or co-op ownership of robots.

steps.text: Volunteer for the council's robot or telecare pilot
Study care robot systems with AI every night
Take extra weekend calls to build a two-month cushion
Campaign for council or co-op ownership of care robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's long enough to get properly qualified in something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before about public ownership. But I'd also say, out loud, that carers should start retraining now, not when the robots turn up in 2034. I'd probably start a group chat for carers along the coast to share courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough to land one of the robot technician jobs if I start now. The office jobs go in 2031, which isn't me. My worry is the course costs and losing hours to study when I'm already short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for an evening course in assistive technology at the college in town next September. I'd keep doing full rounds while I study, and pay off all my credit so I'm clean. I'd also start that group chat for Seacliff and Lighthouse carers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, and a bit tired already, picturing the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a council grant for adult learners if you earn under a certain amount, which I definitely do. If not, I'd ask my uncle, who runs a phone repair shop. He'd lend it and probably give me Saturdays too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the group chat actually help anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would help the ones like Bernadette who don't know where to look. People share shifts in group chats already, so why not courses. It costs nothing.

I'd start a **group chat** for coast carers to share courses.
think: I think five years is enough to land a **robot technician** job.
My worry is **course costs** and lost hours while studying.

Pay off **all credit** while keeping full rounds.
Start a **group chat** for Seacliff and Lighthouse carers.

S3.quote: People share shifts in group chats already, so why not courses.
fieldNote: Five years lets him plan a **formal qualification**, not just volunteering.

steps.text: Enrol in the college's evening assistive technology course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years! I'd be thirty-seven. That's loads of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to make the robots work for carers instead of against them. Governments should fund training now and give carers a say in how robots get used. I'd post that a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well. I'd have the tech qualification, maybe even be running a team that sets up home robots by the late 2030s. My one worry is if the good jobs all go to people with degrees, not people who've actually wiped someone's mouth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Seacliff, do the level three now, then the assistive technology course in a couple of years. I'd use AI to build my own guide for families on how to choose care tech. I'd save a little every month, aiming for three months' cushion by thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Genuinely good. It feels like something I'd choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The guide for families: is that a business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe later. At first it's just a free guide to get my name known. If families started paying for advice, great, but I'm not counting on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the good jobs could go to people with degrees. Would you do one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a part-time one in my thirties if the grant covered it. I'd rather prove myself with the hands-on experience. I've done five hundred hoist transfers, which no graduate has.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to make **robots work for carers**.
I'd ask government to **fund training** and give carers a say.
think: I think I'd do well, maybe running a **robot setup team**.

S4.quote: I've done five hundred hoist transfers, which no graduate has.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be racing for a handful of robot jobs with no savings. What would help is a paid route from carer to care-tech roles, with the council or a co-op running it so it's not just whoever has money for a degree.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what carers know that the robot makers don't. I know my client Mr Osei won't eat if you put the plate on his left. No robot company has ever asked me that kind of thing.

biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, racing for a few robot jobs with no savings.
